newsitem.title: CROATIA: Yugoslav foreign minister in Croatia next week.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav foreign minister in Croatia next week.

text.p: Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic will pay his first official visit to Croatia next week under a normalisation treaty that has solidified peace in the Balkans, the Croatian foreign ministry said on Thursday.

Presidents Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and Franjo Tudjman of Croatia established full diplomatic relations on August 23, ending a conflict that began with Croatia's secession from Serbian-led Yugoslavia in 1991.

In signing the treaty, Yugoslavia -- which now consists of Serbia and Montenegro -- also recognised Croatia's sovereignty over the last rebel Serb enclave on its territory, Eastern Slavonia, which is now under transitional U.N. administration.

Milutinovic's talks with Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic will focus on implementing parts of the August normalisation agreement, including the establishment of consulates in Zagreb and Belgrade, an aide to Granic said.
"This is part of the new process of regional stabilisation, the new international order in this part of Europe," said the official, who declined to say what day the talks would be held.
Croatian government sources said Granic would also seek consensus with Milutinovic on when U.N. authorities should formally hand back Eastern Slavonia to Zagreb's rule.

The Croatian government has reluctantly agreed to a recommendation by the U.N. administrator for a three-month extension to the mandate beyond January 15, 1997, with U.N. peace troops to be out by June.
Granic's aide, who asked not to be identified, said the ministers would also try to iron out details on restoring rail and air traffic between Croatia and Yugoslavia.
He told Reuters that the Croats were keen to reopen two air corridors, in the north between Zagreb and Belgrade and in the south between Dubrovnik and the Yugoslav capital.
Foreign citizens are now able to travel the main highway between Zagreb and Belgrade, a busy commercial corridor between central and southeastern Europe before 1991.

But Croatian government sources said cross-border road traffic by local residents must await a thaw in Serb-Croat relations on the grassroots level, where enmity lingering from the 1991-95 war still runs high.
The Croatian foreign ministry official said the issue of 2,600 Croats listed as missing in the 1991-95 war would be high on the agenda in the talks.

Another issue would be steps to improve the political climate in Bosnia following its postwar elections to reunify the country. Yugoslavia and Croatia wield strong influence over Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats.
